title: Water: where it comes from and what we use it for

summary.text: Put dry poha in a little water, and in a few minutes it goes soft. Put the same poha in oil, and it stays hard. Water gets inside things, and oil does not. That is one reason water can do so many jobs: we drink it, cook with it, wash with it, and plants and other animals need it too. Your child tests poha in water and in oil, finds every place water is used at home, and finds out how different animals drink.
summary.art: Three steel katoris on a kitchen counter: soft swollen poha in water, shiny hard poha in oil, and dry poha, with a child's finger pressing the soft one.

intro.hook: Turn on the tap and fill a tumbler. Where was this water yesterday?
intro.text: The water in our tap came through pipes from a tank, a well, a lake or a river. Before that, it fell as rain. All day long, we use water for many jobs. We drink it. We cook rice and dal in it. We wash our hands, our plates and our clothes with it. We pour it on plants, and we leave some out for birds. In this unit we ask: what jobs does water do, and why is water so good at them?
intro.art: A child holding a steel tumbler under a kitchen tap, with a small picture above of rain falling on a lake and pipes leading to the house.

outcomes: By the end I can name five jobs water does for us: drinking, cooking, washing, watering plants, and giving animals a drink.
By the end I can say where tap water comes from: rain, rivers, lakes and wells, then pipes and tanks.
By the end I can say what happened in the poha test: water made the poha soft, but oil did not.
By the end I can say that every living being needs water, and show how some animals drink.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A source is the place something comes from. A water source is a place we get water from.
terms.example: Rain, a river, a lake and a well are all water sources. The tap is the end of a long pipe from one of them.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: rain falling, a river, a lake, and a round stone well.

terms.meaning: A liquid is something that flows and can be poured, and takes the shape of its cup.
terms.example: Water, milk and oil are liquids. A stone and a spoon are not.
terms.art: Water, milk and coconut oil being poured from three small jugs into three glasses.

terms.meaning: To soak means a liquid goes inside something and fills it up.
terms.example: Poha soaks up water and goes soft. Urad dal soaked overnight grows fat.
terms.art: Two spoons of urad dal: dry, small grains on one, and fat, soaked grains on the other.

terms.meaning: Thirsty is how your body feels when it needs water.
terms.example: After running about on a hot day, you feel thirsty, and a glass of water feels very good.
terms.art: A hot, smiling child after playing outside, drinking from a steel tumbler.

explanations.definition: All living beings need water to stay alive. Humans and other animals drink it, and plants take it in through their roots.
explanations.description: More than half of your body is water. You lose some all day, when you breathe out, sweat and go to the toilet. So you need to drink every day, and you feel thirsty when your body needs more. Other animals drink too, each in their own way. A cat laps with her tongue. A cow sucks water up with her lips. An elephant fills their trunk and squirts the water into their mouth. A frog takes in water through their skin. A plant takes in water through their roots.
examples: You feel thirsty after playing on a hot day.
A crow drinks from a bowl of water on a window ledge.
A tulsi plant droops when the soil is dry, and stands up after you water her.
explanations.context: This card says why every living being needs water.
explanations.art: A child, a crow, a cow, an elephant and a tulsi plant, each getting water in their own way.

explanations.definition: Water can soak into many things, like poha, rice, dal, cloth, paper and soil. Oil does not soak into poha or rice.
explanations.description: Dry poha is hard. Put poha in water, and the water soaks into each flake. In a few minutes the poha is soft. Put poha in oil, and the oil only coats the outside, so the poha stays hard. This is why we cook rice and dal in water. The water gets inside each grain, and the heat makes it soft. Frying in hot oil does something else: it makes food crisp, like a papad or a murukku.
examples: Poha in water is soft in a few minutes. Poha in oil stays hard.
Urad dal soaked overnight for idli batter grows fat with water.
Rice cooked in water grows bigger and softer.
explanations.context: This card says what happened in the poha test, and why we cook rice and dal in water.
explanations.art: A close-up of one poha flake in water, with tiny blue arrows going into it, next to a flake in yellow oil with the oil sitting around the outside.

explanations.definition: Water loosens dirt and carries it away. Soap helps water carry away oily dirt.
explanations.description: Dried dal on a plate is hard and sticks tight. When water soaks into the dried dal, it goes soft again and lets go of the plate. Then the water carries it away. That is how washing works, for plates, clothes and your hands. Oily dirt, like oil on your fingers, does not mix with water. Soap holds on to the oil and to the water, so the water can carry the oil away too.
examples: A plate with dried rice is easy to clean after it soaks in water for a few minutes.
Muddy feet get clean under a tap.
Clothes are soaked in soapy water before they are washed.
explanations.context: This card says how water washes things.
explanations.art: A steel plate with dried dal sitting in water, and a child's hand wiping the dal off easily with a cloth.

explanations.description: When the soil is dry, a plant senses the dryness. Their roots grow towards damp soil. Their leaves close tiny holes, called pores, so they lose less water. If the plant stays dry, the leaves droop. Scientists agree that plants sense dry soil and answer it. They argue about how to describe what the plant does.
examples: A pot plant droops on a hot afternoon and stands up again after a drink.
Roots grow towards a damp part of the soil.
A money plant in a glass of water grows long roots into the water.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists who study how plants sense
perspectives.explanation: The plant feels that the soil is dry and chooses what to do. Closing the leaf pores and growing roots towards water are good choices.
Dry soil sets off chemical signals inside the plant. The plant answers the same way every time. They call this a response, not a feeling.

explanations.context: This card asks if plants feel thirsty, and gives two views.
explanations.art: A potted plant with drooping leaves and roots reaching down towards a damp patch of soil at the bottom of the pot.

agreed.evidence: No living being has ever been found that can stay alive and grow with no water at all. Even seeds that wait for years only start to grow when they get water.

agreed.text: Almost all our fresh water comes from rain.
agreed.evidence: Rain fills rivers, lakes and ponds. Some rain soaks into the ground and fills wells. High in the mountains, snow melts into rivers too. When the rains fail, rivers, lakes and wells run low.

agreed.text: Water soaks into poha, rice and dal, and oil does not.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with poha: in water it goes soft in minutes, and in oil it stays hard. Cooks all over the world boil rice and dal in water to make them soft.

challenging.claim: Oil and water are both liquids, so they do the same jobs.
challenging.who: A common guess before people try it
challenging.for: Oil and water both pour, both look wet, and both take the shape of the cup.
challenging.against: In the poha test, water made the poha soft and oil did not. Oil does not mix with water. We cannot drink oil instead of water, or wash plates with oil alone.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that all liquids are alike.

challenging.claim: Fish live in water, so they never drink.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Fish are wet all the time, and we never see a fish lift their head to drink.
challenging.against: Fish in rivers and ponds take in water through their skin and gills, so they hardly need to drink. Fish in the sea do drink sea water, and get rid of the extra salt through their gills.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that fish never drink.

challenging.claim: At home, we use most of our water for drinking.
challenging.for: Drinking water is the water we think about most, and we drink many times a day.
challenging.against: A person drinks only a few tumblers of water a day. Much more water goes into baths, washing clothes and plates, and flushing the toilet.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that most of our water is for drinking.

big_questions.q: The poha in water went soft, but the poha in oil stayed hard. Why can water get in where oil cannot?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when you put a drop of oil on water. Do they mix?

big_questions.q: The water you drink becomes part of you. When does it stop being water and start being you?
big_questions.hint: More than half of your body is water. Where did all that water come from?

big_questions.q: A frog drinks through their skin. What would it be like to drink that way?
big_questions.hint: Think about how your skin feels in a bath. Does any water go in?

big_questions.q: Who does the water in a river belong to: the people, the fish, the trees or the river?
big_questions.hint: Think of everyone who drinks from one river, from the hills to the sea.

story.title: The Big Pot in Madurai
story.note: Meenakshi, Arjun and Ammamma are made up. Many Indian homes fill pots when the water comes in the morning. Urad dal really grows fat when soaked overnight.
text: Meenakshi lived in a small flat in Madurai with her little brother Arjun and their grandmother, Ammamma. Meenakshi was six. Arjun was four.
In their street, the water came in the tap only in the morning. So every morning, Ammamma filled a big steel pot, a kudam, right to the top. 'This pot is our water for the whole day,' she said.
One morning Arjun knocked on the full pot. Bong! 'It is so full,' he said. 'We will never use it all.'
'Let's see,' said Meenakshi. 'I will watch where the water goes today.'

First, Ammamma boiled some water and let it cool in a clay pot. That was for drinking. Meenakshi drank a whole tumbler after her breakfast. Arjun drank half a tumbler, and spilled the other half on his shirt.
Next, Ammamma washed a cup of rice and put it in the cooker with water. She also put a katori of urad dal in water, for tomorrow's idli batter. 'Why does the dal need a bath?' asked Arjun.
'Wait till tonight, and you will see,' said Ammamma.

After lunch, the plates were sticky with rice and rasam. Ammamma poured a little water on each plate and left them for a few minutes. Then the rice slid off with one wipe. Meenakshi scrubbed her own plate. 'The water made the rice let go,' she said.

In the afternoon, Ammamma washed Arjun's shirt. Then Meenakshi carried a small mug of water to the balcony. She poured it slowly onto the jasmine plant and the tulsi. The dry brown soil turned dark. The water disappeared into it. 'The soil drank it,' she said.
Then she filled an old clay saucer with water and put it on the window ledge. 'This is for the crows,' she told Arjun. 'It is hot, and they are thirsty too.'

They waited behind the curtain. A crow landed on the ledge. The crow looked at the children with one shiny eye. Then the crow dipped her beak in the water, lifted her head, and swallowed. Dip, lift, swallow. Arjun held his breath so the crow would not fly away.
In the evening, Arjun ran to the katori of urad dal. 'Ammamma! The dal got fat!' The small black grains had grown big and soft. Arjun pressed one, and it squashed between his fingers.
'The water went inside the dal,' said Meenakshi. 'Like the poha we soak for breakfast. And like the soil on the balcony.'
Ammamma smiled. 'Water goes inside. That is why it can do so many jobs.'
At bedtime, Meenakshi looked into the big pot. There was only a little water left at the bottom.
She counted on her fingers. 'Drinking. Cooking. Washing the plates and the shirt. The plants. The crow.' She held up five fingers.
'One pot did five jobs,' she said.
Arjun was nearly asleep. 'Six,' he said. 'I spilled some on my shirt. That was a bath for my shirt.'
Ammamma laughed. 'Tomorrow morning, the tap will give us more. And the tap gets its water from the rain. So say thank you to the rain.'
Meenakshi looked out of the window at the dark sky. 'Thank you, rain,' she said.
story.epiphany: Meenakshi sees that one pot of water did many jobs in one day, and that water does them by going inside things: the dal, the soil, the stuck rice and her own body.
ask: What were the jobs the water did in Meenakshi's home?
Why did the urad dal grow fat?
Why did Meenakshi put out water for the crow?
art: A grandmother filling a big steel pot from a kitchen tap in the early morning, with a girl and a small boy watching.
A crow on a window ledge dipping their beak into a clay saucer of water, with two children peeping from behind a curtain.
A small boy pressing a fat, soaked urad dal grain between his fingers, with his sister and grandmother smiling beside a katori of dal.

games.title: Water Jobs
games.context: This is a sorting game about the jobs water does. Each card names something water is doing. Players put each card in the right basket: drinking, cooking, washing, plants or animals.

items.f: A girl drinking from a steel tumbler
A baby having a bottle of water
A grandmother drinking from a clay pot
Urad dal soaking for idli batter
Dal cooking in a pressure cooker
Hands being washed under a tap
Plates being washed in the sink
A child watering a tulsi pot
Rain falling on a rice field
A money plant growing in a glass of water
A crow drinking from a clay saucer
A cow drinking from a trough

printables.title: Five baskets to draw on a big sheet
items: A basket with a tumbler drawn on it: Drinking
A basket with a cooking pot: Cooking
A basket with a soap and bubbles: Washing
A basket with a leaf: Plants
A basket with a crow: Animals

rules: Draw the five baskets on a big sheet. Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and read it aloud (or ask the grown-up to). Say what the water is doing.
Put the card on the basket you think is right. Say why.
The grown-up reads the back. If the basket is right, the card stays there.
If it is wrong, the card goes to the bottom of the pile, to try again later.
With two players, take turns one after the other. With four, go round the circle. Everyone is helping to fill the baskets.
When the pile is finished, count each basket. Every basket should have 3 cards. If one has more or less, check it together.

setup.art: A big sheet on the floor with five baskets drawn on it: a tumbler, a pot, soap bubbles, a leaf and a crow.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the five baskets. Mix the cards.

setup.art: A child holding up a card of rice boiling, about to put it in the cooking basket.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card, say the job, and put it in a basket.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 15 cards. 2. Draw the five baskets on a big sheet. 3. Mix the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: Water does many jobs. These five baskets are five jobs. Can you guess which job each basket is for?
flow.kid: Look at the five baskets. Each one is a job that water does.

flow.do: Take turns. Turn over a card, say what the water is doing, and put it in a basket. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: What is the water doing on your card? Which basket does it go in? Why?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. What is the water doing? Put it in a basket.

ask.q: Why does the soaking dal go in the cooking basket?
good: The water goes inside the dal to make it soft for cooking.

flow.do: Count the cards in each basket together. There should be 3 in each. Ask which job your family does most.
flow.say: Which of these jobs does our family do every day?
flow.kid: Which of these jobs does your family do every day?

check.q: A girl pours water on a tulsi pot. Which job is that?
check.why: The water is for the tulsi plant. Plants take in water through their roots.

games.title: Who Drinks How? A pairs game
games.context: This is a memory game about how animals drink. Half the cards show an animal. Half show a way of drinking. Find the pairs that go together.

printables.title: 12 cards to cut out: 6 animals and 6 ways of drinking
items: Fills a trunk and squirts the water into the mouth
Sucks water up like a straw
Sips with a long tube tongue

rules: Lay all 12 cards face down in rows. The back of every card is blank.
Take turns. Turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If an animal and their way of drinking match, keep the pair and have another turn.
If they do not match, turn them back over. The next player has a go.
When all the pairs are found, count your pairs. The player with the most pairs wins. If you are playing together, count the pairs and cheer.
Then act out each way of drinking together.

setup.art: Twelve cards face down in three rows of four on a mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 12 cards face down.

setup.art: A child turning over a card of an elephant and a card saying fills a trunk, with a big smile.
setup.caption: 2. Turn two cards. Is it a pair?

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards. Read every card aloud once. Mix them and lay them face down.
flow.say: Six animals, and six ways to drink. Let's find which way goes with which animal.
flow.kid: Six animals. Six ways to drink. Find the pairs.

flow.do: Play until all the pairs are found. Read each card aloud as it is turned over. Count the pairs at the end.
flow.say: What does your card say? Which animal drinks that way?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they go together?

ask.q: Why does a butterfly need a long tube tongue?
good: To sip from deep inside a flower.

flow.do: Act out each way of drinking together.
flow.say: Every one of these animals needs water. Which way of drinking would you like to try?
flow.kid: Act out each way of drinking.

options: Fills their trunk and squirts the water into their mouth
Like a straw, through their trunk
check.why: An elephant sucks water a little way up their trunk, then curls the trunk and squirts the water into their mouth.

experiments.title: The Poha Test: water, oil or nothing?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put dry poha in three katoris. One gets water, one gets oil, and one gets nothing. After ten minutes, you press, look and taste.
experiments.question: Water and oil are both liquids. Do they both make dry poha soft?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which poha will be soft after ten minutes: the one in water, the one in oil, or the dry one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three katoris get the same poha, from one packet, the same amount, for the same time. The only difference is what we pour on: water, oil, or nothing.

materials.item: thick poha (aval, avalakki, atukulu or chira) from the kitchen
3 small steel katoris or bowls, all the same
3 paper labels with drawings: a water drop, an oil bottle, a cross
a fourth katori and 4 tablespoons of milk, if you want to try one more

schedule.what: Set up the three katoris, guess, wait ten minutes, then press, look and taste.

experiments.record: Draw the three katoris. Colour the soft poha one colour and the hard poha another colour.

setup.art: Three steel katoris in a row, each with two spoons of dry poha and a small drawn label in front: a water drop, an oil bottle and a cross.
setup.caption: 1. Put two spoons of poha in each katori.

setup.art: A child pouring a spoon of water onto the poha in the first katori, and a grown-up pouring oil onto the poha in the second.
setup.caption: 2. Pour water on one, oil on one, and nothing on the third.

setup.art: A child's finger pressing a soft flake of poha flat on a plate, next to a hard shiny flake from the oil katori that has snapped in two.
setup.caption: 3. After ten minutes, press a flake from each katori.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 tablespoons of dry poha in each katori. 2. Put a label in front of each. 3. Let your child pick up a dry flake and press it.
flow.say: This is dry poha. Pick up one flake. Press it between your fingers. Is it hard or soft?
flow.kid: Pick up one flake of dry poha. Press it. Is it hard or soft?

ask.q: What does the dry poha feel like?

flow.parent: Thick poha works best, because thin poha goes soft very fast. Any brand is fine.

flow.do: Show your child the water and the oil. Ask for a guess and a reason for each katori. Write the guesses down for your child.
flow.say: We will pour water on one katori and oil on another. The third gets nothing. After ten minutes, which poha will be soft? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water on one. Oil on one. Nothing on one. Which poha will go soft? Why?

good: The water one, because we soak poha in water at home.
Both the water and the oil, because they are both wet.
None of them, because ten minutes is not long.

flow.parent: Many children guess that oil and water will both soften the poha, because both are wet. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Pour 4 tablespoons of water over the poha in the water katori. 2. Pour 4 tablespoons of oil over the poha in the oil katori. 3. Leave the third katori dry. 4. Stir each one gently once.
flow.say: Pour the water slowly. Now the oil. Make sure every flake gets wet. The third one stays dry.
flow.kid: Pour water on the first poha. Now oil on the second. Leave the third one dry.
flow.parent: Use the same spoon, wiped, for both liquids. The poha should be covered or nearly covered in both katoris.

flow.do: Wait ten minutes. While you wait, look at the katoris from the side every few minutes, and read the story aloud.
flow.say: Look at the katoris from the side. Is anything changing? Is the water going down? Is the oil going down?
flow.kid: Look at the katoris from the side. Is anything changing?

ask.q: What do you see in the water katori?

flow.parent: In the water katori, the flakes swell and turn pale, and the water level drops as the poha soaks it up. In the oil katori, the flakes look shiny and darker, and the oil stays around them.

flow.do: 1. Take one flake from each katori and put them on a plate. 2. Your child presses each flake with a finger. 3. Then let your child taste a flake from the water and the dry katori.
flow.say: Press each flake. Which one squashes? Which one snaps? Now taste the water poha and the dry poha.
flow.kid: Press a flake from each katori. Which one squashes? Which one snaps?

ask.q: The oil was wet too. Why did that poha stay hard?
good: The oil did not go inside.
The oil only stayed on the outside.

check.q: After ten minutes, which poha was soft?
check.why: Water soaked inside each flake, so the poha went soft. The oil only coated the outside, so that poha stayed hard.

flow.parent: The oil poha can be eaten too: it is only poha and oil. If the oil poha feels a little softer at the edges, that is fine. It is still much harder than the water poha.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. If you have milk, try a fourth katori of poha in milk.
flow.say: So, what do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good claim is: water gets inside poha and makes it soft, and oil does not. Poha in milk goes soft too, because milk is mostly water.

experiments.title: The Sticky Plate: does soaking help washing?
experiments.context: In this experiment you let a little dal dry hard on two plates. You wipe one plate dry. You soak the other plate in water first. Then you see which one comes clean.
experiments.question: Dried dal sticks hard to a plate. Does a little water and a few minutes make it easier to wipe off?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which plate will be easier to wipe clean: the dry one, or the one soaked in water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both plates get the same dal, dried for the same time. Both are wiped the same way, with a dry cloth, for the same count. The only difference is the water.

materials.item: cooked dal or rice, left from a meal
a dry cloth or kitchen tissue

schedule.what: Smear the dal, let it dry for an hour or two, then wipe one plate dry and soak the other.

experiments.record: Draw the two plates after wiping. Draw any dal that is left.

setup.art: Two steel plates under a ceiling fan, each with a small smear of yellow dal drying on it.
setup.caption: 1. Smear a little dal on two plates. Let it dry.

setup.art: One plate being wiped with a dry cloth, leaving dried dal behind, and the other plate sitting with a little water on the dal.
setup.caption: 2. Wipe one plate dry. Pour water on the other and wait.

setup.art: A child counting while wiping the soaked plate clean with one cloth.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe the soaked plate and count the wipes.

flow.wait: Leave the plates under the fan for one or two hours.
flow.do: 1. Smear one teaspoon of thick cooked dal on each plate. 2. Spread it into a thin patch. 3. Leave both plates under a fan or in a sunny spot.
flow.say: We are making two sticky plates. Let's leave them to dry, just like plates that wait too long after lunch.
flow.kid: Smear a little dal on each plate. Leave them to dry.
flow.parent: A thin patch dries in an hour or two under a fan. The dal should feel hard when you touch it. If it is still sticky, wait longer, as it may in a humid city.

flow.do: Pour a little water on one plate, just enough to cover the dal. Ask your child to guess, and say why.
flow.say: One plate gets water. The other stays dry. Which plate will be easier to clean? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour water on one plate. Which plate will be easier to clean? Why?

good: The water one, because the water makes the dal soft.
The dry one, because there is no mess.

flow.do: 1. While the wet plate waits, wipe the dry plate with one dry cloth. Count the wipes, up to 10. 2. After five minutes, wipe the wet plate with the other dry cloth, the same way, and count.
flow.say: Wipe the dry plate. Count your wipes. Is the dal coming off? Now wipe the wet plate. Count again.
flow.kid: Wipe the dry plate. Count. Now wipe the wet plate. Count.

ask.q: Which plate came clean with fewer wipes?

flow.parent: The dry plate usually still has dal stuck on after 10 wipes. The soaked dal goes soft and comes off in a few wipes.

flow.do: Put the two plates side by side. Ask your child what the water did to the dal.
flow.say: What did the water do to the dried dal? Remember the poha. Is it the same?
flow.kid: What did the water do to the dal? Was it like the poha?

check.q: Why did the soaked dal come off more easily?
options: The water went inside the dal and made it soft
check.why: The water soaked into the dried dal, just as it soaked into the poha. Soft dal lets go of the plate.

flow.think: Why do we put dirty plates in water if we cannot wash them straight away?

activities.title: Water Hunt at Home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find every place where water is used. For each place, you say what job the water does there.

schedule.what: Walk round the home and find every tap, pot and place where water is used.

activities.record: Draw the place where your family uses the most water.

setup.art: A child walking through a flat with a grown-up, pointing at the kitchen tap, a bathroom bucket and a plant pot on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home. Find every place water is used.

setup.art: A child pointing at the kitchen tap while a grown-up listens.
setup.caption: 2. At each place, say the job the water does.

flow.do: Walk round the home together. Visit the kitchen, the bathroom, the balcony and any water filter or tank. At each place, ask what the water is used for.
flow.say: Let's find every place where we use water. What job does the water do here?
flow.kid: Find every place in your home where water is used. What job does it do there?

ask.q: What is the water for, here in the kitchen?

flow.parent: Look for the water filter or the drinking pot, the kitchen tap, the bathroom tap and bucket, the washing machine or washing stone, plant pots and a pet bowl.

flow.do: Back in one room, ask your child which place uses the most water. Then ask where the water comes from before it reaches the tap.
flow.say: Which place do you think uses the most water? And where does the water come from before the tap?
flow.kid: Which place uses the most water? Where does the water come from before the tap?

ask.q: Where does our tap water come from?

flow.parent: Most homes get water from a tank, a well, a borewell or a city pipe. All of these are filled by rain in the end.

activities.title: How Do Animals Drink? Act it out
activities.context: In this activity you act out how different animals drink. Each animal drinks in their own way.

materials.item: a bowl of water and a straw

schedule.what: Act out how a cat, a crow, a pigeon, an elephant and a frog drink.

setup.art: A child on hands and knees pretending to lap from a bowl like a cat, with a grown-up laughing.
setup.caption: 1. Drink like a cat: lap, lap, lap.

setup.art: A child swinging an arm like an elephant's trunk towards their mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Drink like an elephant: fill your trunk and squirt.

flow.do: Read out each animal one at a time. Your child acts it out. 1. A cat laps with the tongue, very fast. 2. A crow dips the beak, then lifts the head to swallow. 3. A pigeon keeps the beak in the water and sucks, like a straw. 4. An elephant fills the trunk, then squirts the water into the mouth. 5. A frog sits in water and drinks through the skin.
flow.say: A cat drinks with her tongue. Show me. Now a crow: dip, lift, swallow. Now a pigeon: suck through a straw. Now an elephant!
flow.kid: Drink like a cat. Now a crow: dip, lift, swallow. Now a pigeon, with a straw.
flow.parent: Let your child really sip through the straw for the pigeon. For the frog, they can sit still and pretend to soak.

flow.do: Ask your child which animal they liked best. Ask how you drink.
flow.say: Every animal needs water, but they drink in different ways. How do you drink? Which animal is most like you?
flow.kid: How do you drink? Which animal is most like you?

check.why: A frog takes in water through their skin, mostly through the skin on the belly and legs.

activities.title: My Water Tally
activities.context: In this activity you keep count of how many tumblers of water you drink in one day. You make one mark for each tumbler.

materials.item: a sheet of paper stuck on the fridge or wall
a crayon tied to it with string

schedule.what: Make a mark each time you drink a tumbler of water. Count the marks at bedtime.

activities.record: Count your marks at bedtime. Draw that many tumblers.

setup.art: A sheet of paper on a fridge with a drawn tumbler at the top and a crayon hanging on a string.
setup.caption: 1. Stick up a sheet and tie on a crayon.

setup.art: A child drawing a short line on the sheet after drinking from a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Make a mark each time you drink.

flow.do: In the morning, stick up the sheet and tie on the crayon. Show your child how to make one line for each tumbler.
flow.say: Every time you drink a tumbler of water today, make one line here. Let's count tonight.
flow.kid: Each time you drink a tumbler of water, make one line.

flow.do: At bedtime, count the lines together. Ask when your child felt most thirsty.
flow.say: How many lines did you make? When did you feel most thirsty today? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count your lines. When were you most thirsty?
flow.parent: We drink more on hot days. Some water also comes from food, milk and buttermilk.

projects.title: A Water Bowl for Birds
projects.context: In this project you put out a clay saucer of water for birds, on a window ledge or a balcony. You fill it fresh every day for five days, and watch who comes to drink.

materials.item: a clay saucer, or a wide shallow steel plate

materials.qty: about half a tumbler each day

materials.item: paper and crayons for a bird diary

projects.safety: Pour out the old water and fill fresh water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it. A child should not lean out of a window or over a balcony rail: a grown-up places the saucer.

schedule.what: A grown-up places the saucer on a safe ledge. Fill it with water. Watch for 5 minutes.
Pour out the old water. Fill fresh water. Watch for a few minutes.
Fresh water again. Did any bird or insect come?
Fresh water again. Draw any visitor in your diary.
Fresh water. Look at your diary. Who came to drink?

projects.record: Keep a bird diary: each day, draw who came to the bowl, or draw an empty bowl.

setup.art: A grown-up placing a clay saucer of water on a wide window ledge outside a flat, with a child watching from inside.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up places the saucer on a safe ledge.

setup.art: A crow and a myna drinking from a clay saucer on a balcony wall, seen through a window.
setup.caption: 2. Fill it fresh each day. Watch who comes.

flow.do: 1. Choose a ledge or a balcony wall that birds can reach. 2. A grown-up puts the saucer there. 3. Fill it with water. 4. Watch quietly from inside for 5 minutes.
flow.say: Birds get thirsty too, especially in hot weather. Let's give them a place to drink. Who do you think will come?
flow.kid: A grown-up puts the bowl out. You fill it. Who will come to drink?
flow.parent: Birds may take a few days to find a new bowl. A quiet place with a perch nearby works best.

flow.wait: Come back each day for three more days.
flow.do: Each day, pour out the old water and fill fresh. Watch for a few minutes. Draw any visitor in the diary.
flow.say: Who came today? How did they drink? Did they drink, or have a bath?
flow.kid: Fill fresh water. Watch. Who came? Draw them.

good: Dipped the beak and lifted the head.
Took a sip and looked up.

flow.parent: Crows, mynas, pigeons, bulbuls and sparrows often come, and bees and wasps too in hot weather. If nobody comes in 5 days, try a different spot, or keep going: some bowls take a week to be found.

flow.do: On day 5, look at the diary together.
flow.say: Look at all the days. Who came the most? Why do you think birds need our water bowl in a city?
flow.kid: Look at your diary. Who came the most?
flow.think: Where did birds drink before there were buildings here?

challenges.title: Water the Plant While We Are Away
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Your family is going away for two days. Who will water the plant? Can you make something that waters a pot plant while nobody is home?
challenges.problem: A pot plant needs water every day. Make something from home things that keeps the soil damp while nobody is home for two days. Test it for one day.
constraints: The soil must still be damp after one day.
materials: a plastic bottle or a steel tumbler of water
a thick cotton string, a strip of old cotton cloth, or a cotton wick from a lamp
a few books or a box to stand the water on
general: Fill a plastic bottle with water, poke a small hole in the cap, and push it upside down into the soil, so the water drips out slowly.
Put the pot on a plate with a little water, so the soil drinks from the bottom.
creative: Put one end of a wet cotton string in a tumbler of water and push the other end into the soil. The water creeps along the string into the pot.
Cover the soil with a layer of dry leaves or paper, so less water dries away.
Put the plant in the shade for two days, so the soil dries more slowly.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own plant waterer. Draw it, make it, and test it for one day. Is the soil still damp?

setup.art: A tumbler of water standing on two books next to a pot plant, with a wet cotton string running from the water into the soil.
setup.caption: 1. Run a wet cotton string from a tumbler into the soil.

setup.art: A child pressing a finger into dark, damp soil the next day, next to a tumbler with less water in it.
setup.caption: 2. The next day, feel the soil. Is it damp?

flow.do: Show your child the pot plant and say the problem. Look at the ideas together.
flow.say: We are going away for two days. Who will give our plant water? Can we make something that waters the plant while we are away?
flow.kid: Your family is going away. How can the plant get water while you are gone?

flow.do: 1. Your child picks an idea or invents one. 2. Help build it. If you have a second pot, water it the same and give it no help, to compare. For the string waterer, wet the string first and stand the tumbler higher than the pot.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? Let's make it.
flow.kid: Pick an idea. Make it with a grown-up.
flow.parent: A grown-up pokes any holes in bottle caps. The string idea works best with thick cotton string, wetted first, with the tumbler on books so the water is higher than the soil.

flow.do: The next day, feel the soil and look at the water level.
flow.say: Is the soil still damp? Did the water go down? Where did it go?
flow.kid: Feel the soil. Is it damp? Did the water go down?

good: Along the string into the soil.
Into the soil, and the plant drank some.

items.p: Circle in blue the things that need water. Cross out the things that do not.
items.why: Every living being needs water: crows, plants, cows and you. A stone and a spoon are not alive, so they do not drink.
items.art: Six small pictures: a crow, a tulsi pot, a child, a stone, a steel spoon and a cow.

items.p: In the poha test, one katori got nothing. Why did we keep a katori with nothing?
opts: To see what dry poha does by itself
Because we ran out of water
items.why: The katori with nothing shows what poha does on its own. Then we know the water or the oil made the change.

items.p: Draw one flake of poha from the water katori and one from the oil katori. Show which one squashed.
items.a: A fat, soft, squashed flake for water. A flat, shiny, hard flake for oil.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water flake bigger and squashed, and the oil flake still flat and hard.
items.art: Two empty circles, one with a water drop above it and one with an oil bottle above it.

items.p: Draw a line from each picture to the job water is doing.
pairs: Rice in a pot of boiling water
Water poured on a jasmine pot
items.why: Each picture shows one job: rice cooks in water, hands get washed, the girl drinks, and the jasmine plant takes in water through their roots.
items.art: Four pictures on the left: rice boiling, hands under a tap, a girl with a tumbler, a jasmine pot being watered. Four words on the right.

items.p: Here is a picture of rain, a lake, a pipe and a tap. Write 1, 2, 3 and 4 to show the way the water goes, from first to last.
items.why: Rain fills the lake. Pipes carry the lake water to our homes. Then it comes out of the tap.
items.art: Four pictures in a mixed-up order: a tap, rain falling, a pipe, a lake. Each has an empty box for a number.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why do we cook rice in water and not in oil?
items.a: Water goes inside the rice and makes it soft. Oil does not go inside.
items.why: A strong answer uses the poha test: water soaked into the poha and oil did not.

items.p: Plants take in water through their ____.
items.why: A plant's roots are in the soil. They take in the water that soaks into the soil.

items.p: Which one is NOT a water source?
items.why: A water source is a place we get water from. Rain, rivers and wells give us water. A bag of rice does not.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi are washing plates after lunch. The rice on the plates has dried hard.

views.says: Let's soak the plates in a little water first, and wait.
Let's just scrub hard with a dry cloth. It is quicker.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you saw in the sticky plate test. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Kavya is closer: the soaked plate came clean in a few wipes. But Farhan is right that soaking takes a few minutes of waiting.
items.why: A strong answer uses the sticky plate result, and is fair to both: soaking makes cleaning easier, but it takes a little time.

items.p: Water does only one job: we drink it.
items.why: False. Water also cooks our food, washes things, helps plants grow and gives animals a drink.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, puts poha in milk for breakfast. After ten minutes, what will the poha be like?
opts: Soft, because milk is mostly water
Shiny and hard, like poha in oil
items.why: Milk is mostly water. The water in the milk soaks into the poha and makes it soft.

items.p: Thirsty is how your body feels when it needs ____.
items.why: You feel thirsty when your body needs more water.

items.p: Rain fills rivers, lakes and ____ with water.
items.why: Rain soaks into the ground and fills wells, as well as rivers and lakes.

items.p: Put the urad dal pictures in order, from first to last.
items.why: First the dal is dry. Then it sits in water. The water goes inside, and the dal grows fat and soft.
items.art: Three pictures in mixed-up order: fat soft dal, dry dal in a katori, and dal under water.

items.p: Draw your home. Draw every place where your family uses water.
items.a: A drawing with the kitchen tap, the bathroom, the drinking pot or filter, and plants or a pet bowl.
items.why: A strong drawing shows water used for at least three different jobs.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a dry flower pot gets a mug of water. Where does the water go?
items.a: It soaks into the soil, and the plant's roots take the water in. Some drips out of the hole at the bottom.
items.why: A strong answer says the soil soaks up the water, like the poha did, and the plant takes the water in through the roots.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why do people put out bowls of water for birds in the summer?
items.a: Birds need water too. In hot weather, many puddles and ponds dry up, so it is hard for birds to find a drink in a city.
items.why: A strong answer says that birds need water like we do, and that in a hot city water is hard to find.

items.p: Our tap water came out of a pipe. Where did the water in the pipe come from first?
opts: From rain, which fills lakes, rivers and wells
items.why: Pipes bring water from tanks, lakes, rivers and wells. All of them are filled by rain.

items.p: Three people in Puducherry talk about the best way to use one bucket of water.

views.says: Drinking and cooking come first. People cannot live without them.
Save some for the plants. They give us food and shade.
Save some for the birds. They cannot turn on a tap.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Say why. Then say one good thing about another person's idea.
items.a: Any choice with a reason is fine. For example: Revathi, because people need water to live. But Priya is right that birds need water too and cannot get it from a tap.
items.why: A strong answer picks one person, gives a reason, and is fair to another view. Every living being needs water, so there is no single right answer.

items.p: The water you drink becomes part of your body.
items.why: True. More than half of your body is water, and you need to drink every day to keep it so.

videos.title: A cat lapping water, filmed in slow motion
videos.why: Shows how a cat pulls up a little column of water with the tip of the tongue, as the scientists in 2010 saw.
videos.check: Find a real slow-motion video. Check it shows the tongue touching the top of the water, not scooping.

videos.title: An elephant drinking with their trunk
videos.why: Shows an elephant filling the trunk and squirting water into the mouth.
videos.check: Find a real video of an elephant drinking, ideally an Asian elephant in India. Check the water goes into the mouth, not just a bath.

videos.title: Poha soaking in water, close up
videos.why: Shows poha flakes swelling as water soaks in, for families who cannot do the test today.
videos.check: Find a short cooking video that shows dry and soaked poha side by side. Check it shows real soaking, not cooking with heat.

quiz.p: Which of these is a job that water does for us?
quiz.why: We cook rice in water. Water also helps us drink, wash, and give plants and animals what they need.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT a job for water at home?
quiz.why: We sharpen a pencil with a sharpener, not with water. Washing plates and watering plants both need water.

quiz.p: Where does the water in our tap come from, before the pipes?
opts: From rain, rivers, lakes and wells
quiz.why: The tap is only the end of a pipe. The water comes from tanks, lakes, rivers and wells, which are filled by rain.

quiz.p: Which one is a water source?
quiz.why: A water source is a place we get water from. A lake holds rain water.

quiz.p: Poha sat in oil for ten minutes. What was it like?
quiz.why: Oil does not go inside poha. It only coats the outside, so the poha stays hard.

quiz.p: Why did the poha in water go soft?
opts: The water went inside each flake
quiz.why: Water soaks into poha. The water was not hot, and all the katoris were the same.

quiz.p: Which of these needs water to live?
quiz.why: A plant is alive and needs water. A spoon and a stone are not alive.
A cat laps with her tongue, very fast. Each lap pulls up a little water.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, guesses that oil will make poha soft. What should he do to find out?
quiz.why: The best way to find out is to test it: put poha in oil, wait, and press it.

quiz.p: In the poha test, why do all three katoris get the same poha?
quiz.why: If only the liquid is different, we know the liquid made the difference.

applications: Cooks soak rice, dal, rajma and chana before cooking, so water gets in and they cook faster.
Farmers sow seeds when the monsoon rains come, and some fields are watered from canals and wells.
In summer, many people in Indian cities put out pots of water for birds, and shops in some towns keep a matka of water for anyone who is thirsty.
People in many villages build small walls across streams, called check dams, to hold rain water so wells stay full. In Rajasthan, Amla Ruia has helped villages build many of them.

open_questions.q: What does thirst feel like for a plant?
open_questions.why_open: Plants sense dry soil and act on it. But nobody knows what that feeling is like for a plant.

open_questions.q: Where did Earth's water first come from?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think most of it came from rocks that made the Earth. Others think much of it came later, from icy comets and rocks from space. They are still testing both ideas.

open_questions.q: How do some desert animals live for a long time without drinking?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the tricks, like getting water from food. But they are still finding new ones in animals that have not been studied much.

ask_kids: What did you use water for today?
Where do you think the crow outside drinks?
Is there water inside the food on your plate? Which food has the most?
If the tap stopped for a day, which job would you save water for first?
When did you feel thirsty today?

What did the oil say to the poha?
jokes.a: Sorry, I can't get through to you!

jokes.j: Why did the urad dal grow so fat?
What did the crow say at the water bowl?
jokes.a: This one is on the house!

maths.problem: Gurpreet fills a jug with water, one small tumbler at a time. She counts each tumbler as she pours: 1, 2, 3, 4. Then the jug is full. How many tumblers does the jug hold?
maths.explain: She counted one tumbler each time she poured, and stopped at 4 when the jug was full. A bigger jug would hold more tumblers. A smaller tumbler would need more pours to fill the same jug.
maths.context: This is about the water tally, where you count tumblers of water.
maths.why_maths: Counting tumblers tells us how much a jug holds, and how much water we drink.

maths.problem: Divya is a girl in Class 1. On Monday, she drank 5 tumblers of water. On Tuesday, after playing in the sun, she drank 7. On which day did she drink more? Why do you think so?
maths.explain: 7 is 2 more than 5. On Tuesday she played in the sun and lost more water by sweating, so she felt more thirsty.
maths.context: This is about the water tally, where you make one mark for each tumbler you drink.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two days shows that we drink more when we lose more water.

maths.problem: In the Water Jobs game, Bhavna, a girl in Class 1, sorted the cards. Drinking got 3, Cooking 3, Washing 3, Plants 3 and Animals 3. How many cards did she sort?
maths.explain: 3 and 3 is 6. 6 and 3 is 9. 9 and 3 is 12. 12 and 3 is 15. Five jobs with 3 cards each make 15.
maths.context: This is about the Water Jobs game, where you sort cards into five baskets.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the baskets checks that every card was sorted into a job.

maths.problem: Over 5 days, the bird bowl had these visitors: 2 crows, 1 myna, 3 pigeons and 1 bulbul. Make one tally mark for each bird. Which bird came most?
maths.explain: Crows: 2 marks. Myna: 1 mark. Pigeons: 3 marks. Bulbul: 1 mark. The longest row of marks is the pigeons.
maths.context: This is about the bird bowl project, where you watch who comes to drink.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let us see at a glance which bird visited most often.

founder: ideas/by_topic/water.md: the cooling sheetali breath idea ('notice moisture in exhale') is used in the Roots practice. The notebook's other water ideas (clouds, monsoon, buoyancy, underwater sound) belong to other units. Its drip-drip relay was not used, because Level 3 of this subtopic already has a water-carrying activity.
science: Starch in rice and poha takes up water (hydration and, with heat, gelatinisation). Oil does not hydrate starch, so poha in oil stays hard. Frying makes food crisp because hot oil drives water out. Any food science textbook, for example Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking.
The human body is more than half water (about 60 percent in adults, a little more in children).

Reis, Jung, Aristoff and Stocker, 'How cats lap: water uptake by Felis catus', Science 330 (2010): 1231-1234. Cats touch the water with the tip of the curled-back tongue and pull up a column of water, then close the mouth. Big cats lap more slowly.
Pigeons and doves drink by suction without lifting the head. Most other birds, including crows, scoop and tilt the head back.
Elephants suck water part way up the trunk and squirt it into the mouth.
Most frogs absorb water through the skin, especially a patch on the belly and thighs, and rarely drink by mouth.
Freshwater fish gain water through the gills and skin and drink little. Sea fish drink sea water and get rid of salt through the gills.
Plants sense soil drying, close their stomata (leaf pores), and roots can grow towards moisture (hydrotropism).
Thirukkural 20 (chapter 2, The Excellence of Rain). Tao Te Ching, chapter 8.
Rani ki Vav, Patan: built in the 11th century, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.
Amla Ruia and the Aakar Charitable Trust: check dams in Rajasthan villages.

roots.context: We have seen water soak into poha, dal and soil, and seen many animals drink. Now we ask what that tells us about water, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In our poha test, the poha in water went soft within minutes. The poha in oil went shiny but stayed hard. Water slipped inside each flake, and oil only coated the outside. That is why we cook rice and dal in water, not in oil.
deep_truth.habit: We think all runny, wet things are alike. Water and oil both pour and both look wet, but only water gets inside the poha, and that difference is what makes water able to cook and wash.
deep_truth.evidence: In the poha test, the same poha, for the same time, went soft in water and stayed hard in oil and in the dry katori. In the sticky plate test, dried dal went soft and let go of the plate only after water soaked into it.

three.who_am_i: More than half of you is water. The water you drank this morning is part of you now.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs water: you, the crow, the tulsi and the frog. Each one takes it in their own way.
three.what_is_this_world: The same rain fills the rivers, the wells, the plants and our tumblers. One water is shared by everyone who lives here.

roots.thread: One rain falls on the land. Some goes into a river, some into a well, some into a tulsi pot. From there it goes into a crow, a cow, a pot of rice and you. The same water does many jobs, because it can get inside so many different things.

teachings.teaching: The world cannot go on without water, and without rain, the right order of life cannot go on.
teachings.link: Every job we found for water, from drinking to cooking to the crow's bowl, starts with rain filling our rivers and wells.

teachings.teaching: The highest goodness is like water. Water helps all living things, and does not fight with them. It goes to the low places that others avoid.
teachings.link: Water helps everyone who needs it: the poha in the pot, the tulsi, the crow and you.

science.text: More than half of your body is water. You lose some every day in your breath, sweat and urine, so you need to drink every day.
Plants sense dry soil, close their leaf pores and grow roots towards water. What thirst feels like for a plant, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Many scientists say water is simply a substance that moves by the rules of physics and chemistry. It soaks into poha because of how its tiny particles stick to the poha, and they would not call that giving or helping.

practice.title: Cool breath, warm breath
practice.say: Curl your tongue like a tube, if you can, and breathe in slowly through it. Feel the cool air. Now close your mouth and breathe out through your nose onto the back of your hand. Is it warm? Is it a little damp? That damp is water leaving your body. Now take one slow sip from your tumbler. Feel it go down.
practice.kid: Curl your tongue like a tube. Breathe in slowly. Feel the cool air. Breathe out onto your hand. Is it damp? Now take one slow sip of water.

ask: The water you sip becomes part of you. Was it ever part of a cloud, a river or a plant?
Water made the poha soft, but oil could not. What else can water do that oil cannot?
Who needs the water in our tap more: us, the tulsi, or the crow?
roots.art: A child sipping from a steel tumbler by a window, with a crow drinking from a clay saucer on the ledge and a tulsi pot beside them, and rain clouds in the sky beyond.

how_we_found_out.context: How does a cat drink? This card tells the true story of how scientists found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought a cat drinks by curling the tongue into a little spoon and scooping water up. A cat laps so fast that nobody could see for sure. In 2010, four scientists in the United States, Pedro Reis, Sunny Jung, Jeffrey Aristoff and Roman Stocker, decided to look properly. They filmed cats drinking with very fast cameras, and played the films back slowly. The tongue was not a spoon at all. The cat curls the tip of the tongue back and touches the top of the water lightly, without dipping in. Then the cat pulls the tongue up very fast. The water sticks to the tongue and is pulled up into a little column. Before the column falls back, the cat closes her mouth and catches the top of the column. A pet cat does this about four times every second. The scientists also watched films of lions and tigers, and found that bigger cats lap more slowly.
how_we_found_out.who: Pedro Reis, Sunny Jung, Jeffrey Aristoff and Roman Stocker, scientists in the United States
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a cat scoops water up with the tongue like a spoon. Slow-motion films showed that the tongue only touches the top of the water and pulls up a column, which the cat bites off.
how_we_found_out.art: A slow-motion picture of a cat's tongue lifting a thin column of water from a bowl, with the cat's mouth about to close on the column.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and child in a flat. The Water Jobs cards now say the end state (3 in each basket), the pairs game no longer prints the answers on the backs of cards, and both games now have a clear end and a winner for 2 or 4 players. The poha wait no longer says to play a 15-minute game in a 10-minute wait, the Water Hunt no longer mentions slips that no step used, and the bird saucer, string waterer and sticky plate all work with home things. Removed one weak joke, repeated worksheet questions (replaced with new ones), the plant-feels-thirst line that contradicted the debate, and fixed the crow's pronouns and unclear maths and quiz names. Second pass: the quiz no longer names Arjun as guessing about poha (he never does in the story), the bird bowl wait now matches the days on the schedule, the sticky plate uses one cloth for each plate and thick cooked dal, the plant waterer says to keep an unhelped pot for comparison, a repeated 'water source' question and an unsourced drinking number were replaced, the elephant joke was made a real joke. The three videos still have no checked address, so they stay marked as to find.
